title: The bait
hookLine: the deer-feeder's crops, laid out to catch four herds
last: RELAY CHARIOTS — ONE STAGE AT A TIME.

lines: FREE, BRIGHT, A GIFT EVERY MORNING.
A FIELD, AND A HERD OF DEER.
cards: A phone game is free. The first level is easy, the colors are bright, and there's a little gift waiting every morning if you open it. Nobody built that by accident.
Somebody sat in a room and planned how you'd be caught, gently, so you'd never feel the net. Twenty-five centuries ago the Buddha described the same room, only with a field and a herd of deer.

teach.h: A CROP PLANTED TO CATCH DEER
teach.b: In the twenty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, a deer-feeder plants a crop, not out of kindness, but so deer will come, eat carelessly, and be easy to catch. Four herds come.
The first walks straight into the crop, eats without care, grows heedless, and is caught. The second sees this and swears off the crop entirely.
They go deep into the forest and live on wild grass, but in the last month of the hot season the grass and water run out. Thin and weak, they wander back, eat wildly, and are caught too.

The third herd makes a lair close by and eats carefully, never losing its head. But the deer-feeder notices them, puts up a great fence around the field, finds where they sleep, and catches them as well.
The fourth herd makes its lair where the deer-feeder can't go. They eat without losing their heads, and slip away; the feeder and his men can't find them. Then the Buddha explains.
The crop is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at us. The deer-feeder is Mara, the tempter.

teach.h: FOUR HERDS: DIVE IN, RUN, HOVER, ESCAPE
teach.b: The herds are four kinds of seekers: those who dive in, those who run to harsh denial and break, those who stay close and get trapped by opinions, and those who go where Mara can't follow, into deep stillness.

teach.h: THE CROP IS THE FIVE CORDS OF PLEASURE

teach.b: Starving wasn't freedom. The way out is neither the crop nor the desert. It's eating without being caught.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the Nivapa Sutta's four herds to describe the middle way between indulgence and harsh denial; monastics and lay meditators practice restraint of the senses and deep concentration as the 'lair' Mara can't reach.

o: a crop planted so deer eat carelessly
a gift of food left out for wild deer
a lure a fisherman ties to his line

games.q: the four herds — tap the pairs.
p: fled to the forest, starved, came back
ate carefully nearby, but was fenced in
went where the feeder couldn't follow

s: the herd that gave up the crop completely escaped
the second herd starved in the hot season, came back weak, and was caught.
the crop is the five cords of sense pleasure, and the feeder is Mara.
the crop was planted to feed the deer
it was planted so the deer would grow careless and be easy to catch.

games.q: you're a deer. you've watched the first herd get caught in the crop. what do you do?
o: never touch the crop again, and live on wild grass.
eat carefully, from a lair close by.
eat without losing your head, from a lair the feeder can't reach.
games.why: the second herd starved and came back; the third was fenced in. only the fourth herd, eating without infatuation where the feeder couldn't go, slipped away.

practice: Think of the last time today you reached for something without deciding to, the phone, the fridge, the feed, the cart, and without judging it, see the field it grew in and how bright it looked.
Then come back to the breath, which nobody is selling you, and if the pull comes again, watch it rise like a deer lifting its head, and stay where you are.

wordCard.voice: The bait. The deer-feeder's crop: pleasures laid out on purpose, so we'll eat carelessly and be caught.

orig.note: Pali nivapa: bait, fodder laid out. the discourse is the Nivapa Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: the bait is set. The fourth herd ate, and still slipped away. Day four hundred twenty-three, done.
